(p-171)In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah An-Nas

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾ ﴿the King of mankind﴾ ﴿the God of mankind﴾.

Earlier, in his commentary on His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That you worship none but Allah. Indeed I am to you from Him a warner and a bringer of good tidings﴾ [Hud: 2], in Surah Hud, the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on us and on him, referred the reader to this surah. He said about that verse: "It contains clear evidence that the greatest wisdom for which the Qur'an was revealed is that Allah, may He be exalted, be worshipped alone, and that nothing be associated with Him in His worship."

He then cited verses similar to it and said: "We have pointed to this topic in Surah al-Fatihah, and we will fully examine it, if Allah the Exalted wills, in Surah an-Nas, so that this blessed book may end well." End of quotation.

In this reference by him, may Allah have mercy on us and on him, there is an alert to the meanings contained in this noble surah, and a direction to observe that conclusion.

Likewise, in that reference there is a burden of thorough investigation, since he did not rest content with what he had presented in Surah al-Fatihah, nor with what he had presented in Surah Hud, but made the full investigation to be in this surah. The meaning of "istiqsa'" (thorough investigation) is comprehensiveness to the utmost limit.

I do not think anyone can thoroughly investigate what another intends, especially what the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on us and on him, intended, and what he himself was able to do.

However, as we stated at the beginning, this is the effort of one of limited means and the full extent of capacity. So we seek Allah's help and ask Him for guidance, taking direction from what the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on us and on him, presented in the surahs al-Fatihah and Hud. Then we present a viewpoint on the two surahs together, al-Falaq and an-Nas, and then from them and in the order of the noble Mushaf (the written Qur'an), hoping for and seeking Allah's success and assistance.

(p-172) As for the reference, what appears is that its reason is that in this noble surah three attributes of Allah, the Exalted, of greatness and perfection have come together: "Lord of mankind," "King of mankind," "God of mankind." It seems that at first glance they point to the Lord, the King, who is the true God deserving to be worshipped alone.

Perhaps this is also what the content of the preceding surah, al-Ikhlas, guides to: "He is Allah, the One. Allah, the Eternal Refuge." This is the logic of reason and the true word, because the requirement of sovereignty entails servitude, and servitude entails divinity and the affirmation of Oneness in divinity (tawhid al-uluhiyyah). For a owned servant (al-'abd al-mamluk) is obliged to obey and listen to his owner merely by virtue of ownership, even if his owner is a servant like himself. How much more so is the servant owned by his Lord and God, and how much more so is the owner who is the one, unique, single, eternal God?

These three attributes, Lord, King, God, have come in the opening of the first of the Mushaf: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ ﴿the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾ [al-Fatihah: 2-4]. The other recitation (qira'ah) is "King of the Day of Judgement" [al-Fatihah: 4].

In the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah there is the first call addressed to mankind to worship Allah alone, because He is their Lord, along with a statement of the reasons for that in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21].

Then He explained the reason for that in His saying: ﴿who created you and those before you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21].

And in His saying: ﴿who made the earth for you a bed and the sky a canopy, and sent down from the sky water and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 22].

All of this is among the effects of lordship (rububiyyah) and of His right over His creation to be worshipped. Then He explained the requirement of singling Him out alone for that in His saying: ﴿So do not attribute to Allah equals while you know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 22].

That is: just as He has no equal in creation, nor in provision, nor in anything mentioned, so do not attribute to Allah equals also in worship, while you know the reality of that.

The worship of Him alone and the negation of equals is what the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on us and on him, described as: the meaning of "There is no god but Allah" by negation and affirmation (nafyan wa ithbatan).

So the affirmation is in His saying: ﴿and worship Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 72].

(p-173) And the negation is in His saying: ﴿So do not attribute to Allah equals﴾.

That lordship necessitates worship came explicitly in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾ ﴿who fed them against hunger and secured them against fear﴾ [Quraysh: 3-4].

So the relative pronoun and its clause carry the sense of giving a reason for the requirement of worship. More explanation of this will come, if Allah the Exalted wills, at the end of the surah.

Here the phrase "Lord of mankind" has come, with the Lord attributed to mankind, which conveys particularity, although He, glory be to Him, is Lord of the worlds and Lord of everything, as in the opening of al-Fatihah: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾.

And in His saying: ﴿Say: Should I seek a lord other than Allah while He is the Lord of everything?﴾ [al-An'am: 164].

So the attribution here is to some individuals of the general category.

He has also been attributed to some other individuals, such as the heavens and the earth and others, from some of everything, as in His saying: ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth? Say: Allah﴾ [al-Ra'd: 16].

And His saying: ﴿Lord of the East and the West; there is no god but He, so take Him as a trustee﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 9].

And to the House: ﴿So let them worship the Lord of this House﴾ [Quraysh: 3].

And to the sacred land: ﴿I have only been commanded to worship the Lord of this city﴾ [al-Naml: 91].

And to the Throne: ﴿Lord of the Noble Throne﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 116].

And to the Messenger: ﴿Follow what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 106].

And His saying: ﴿And your Lord, so glorify﴾ [Muhammad: 3], and other than that.

But it is noted that with every attribution of this kind there is what conveys generality, and that with its attribution to an individual of the general category, He is still Lord of the worlds and Lord of everything. So with its attribution to the heavens and the earth, there came with it "Say: Allah."

With the attribution to East and West, there came ﴿there is no god but He, so take Him as a trustee﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 9].

(p-174) With the attribution to the House, there came: ﴿who fed them against hunger and secured them against fear﴾.

With the attribution to the city, there came ﴿who made it sacred﴾ [al-Naml: 91], and He is Allah, the Exalted.

With the attribution to the Throne, there came His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Exalted is Allah, the True King; there is no god but He, Lord of the Noble Throne﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 116].

With the attribution to the Messenger (ﷺ), there came His saying: ﴿Your Lord has not forsaken you﴾ [al-Duha: 3], and other than that. Every attribution to any individual of the general category comes with what conveys generality, and that Allah is Lord of the worlds.

Here "Lord of mankind" has come with: ﴿King of mankind﴾ ﴿God of mankind﴾, to convey generality also; because the word "Lord" may be shared by a master who is obeyed, as in His saying: ﴿They took their rabbis and their monks as lords besides Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 31].

And Yusuf's saying to his companion in prison: ﴿Mention me before your lord﴾ [Yusuf: 42], meaning the king according to the most apparent opinions, and His saying: ﴿Return to your lord and ask him what is the matter with the women﴾, the verse [Yusuf: 50].

So He brought "King" and "God" to indicate generality, in the sense of "Lord of mankind." He, glory be to Him, is Lord of the worlds and Lord of everything. But His attribution here to mankind specifically is an indication of further particularity, and the Lord's care, glory be to Him, for His servant whom He called to Himself so that he might seek refuge in Him from his enemy. Also in it is a strengthening of the servant's hope in his Lord, that He, glory be to Him, by His lordship will protect His servant because of his servanthood and will shield him from what he has sought refuge from.

This particularity is further strengthened by the attribution of the Lord to the Messenger (ﷺ) in all his stages since the two beginnings: the beginning of creation and the beginning of revelation, in His saying: ﴿Read in the name of your Lord who created﴾ ﴿created man from a clinging substance﴾ [al-'Alaq: 1-2]; then in his upbringing: ﴿Your Lord has not forsaken you, nor has He detested﴾, up to His saying ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge?﴾ ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾ ﴿And He found you poor and made you self-sufficient﴾ [al-Duha: 3-8].

And He made the turning to Him in the surah after it: ﴿And to your Lord turn with longing﴾ [al-Sharh: 8], enumerating the blessings upon him: the expansion of the breast, the removal of the burden, the raising of his mention; then at the end His saying: ﴿Indeed, to your Lord is the return﴾ [al-'Alaq: 8].

(p-175) His saying, ﴿Malik an-nas﴾ (the King of mankind). In placing "King of mankind" after "Lord of mankind," there is a gradual progression in alerting the listener to these great meanings, and a movement of the servants from the starting point of faith in the Lord, because of the signs of lordship (rububiyyah, the Lord's sole governance of creation) they have witnessed in creation, provision, and all of those beings. This is as was mentioned in the first address directed to them: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may become righteous﴾ ﴿Who made for you the earth a bed and the sky a canopy, and sent down from the sky water and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:21–22).

All these signs, which they have touched and acknowledged as necessitating that the One who brought them into being is their Lord, then move them to the second level, which is that the Lord whose acts these are is their King, the one who disposes of those worlds, the sovereign over His command and all His affairs, and the King of the affairs of this world and the Hereafter together.

When the one who affirms this reaches this realization, he necessarily acknowledges that He alone is the Deity (uluhiyyah, the state of being the sole object of worship), which is the final rank.

﴿Ilah an-nas﴾ (the God of mankind), i.e., their object of worship (ma'luhihim) and the one they worship, which is the purpose for which He created them: ﴿And I did not create the jinn and mankind except that they should worship Me﴾ (Adh-Dhariyat 51:56).

In the attribution of the King to mankind there is an indication of specialization (ikhtisas), although He, glorified is He, is the King of everything. It has what the attribution of the Lord to mankind has, whose discussion has preceded. He, glorified is He, is the Owner of the sovereignty (malik al-mulk), as in His saying: ﴿Say, "O Allah, Owner of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will, and You honor whom You will and You humble whom You will"﴾ (Ali 'Imran 3:26).

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Him belongs the dominion, and to Him belongs all praise﴾ (At-Taghabun 64:1).

And His saying: ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:107), and His saying: ﴿The King, the Pure﴾ (Al-Hashr 59:23).

So He, glorified and exalted is He, is the one singular in sovereignty, having no partner in His dominion, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And say, "All praise is due to Allah, who has not taken a son and has not had a partner in dominion"﴾ (Al-Isra' 17:111). He began with praise first.

Similar to it is His saying: ﴿So exalted is He in whose hand is the realm of all things﴾ (Ya-Sin 36:83). He began with glorifying Himself and declaring Him free of imperfection, for the generality of dominion, the absoluteness of disposal, and the negation of a partner; because His dominion is a dominion of disposal and management together with perfection in praise and sanctification.

(p-176) And like His saying: ﴿Blessed is He in whose hand is the dominion, and He is over all things competent﴾ (Al-Mulk 67:1).

Through these texts it becomes known that the dominion of Allah, exalted is He, is perfect, and that the dominion of anything other than Him, of the kings of this world, is deficient. We know that their dominion is by Allah's granting it to them, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah gives His dominion to whom He wills﴾ (Ali 'Imran 3:26).

And His saying: ﴿Say, "O Allah, Owner of sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will"﴾ (Ali 'Imran 3:26).

It is known that the kings of this world have a dominion of governance and guardianship, not a dominion of ownership and disposal. As in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And their prophet said to them, "Indeed, Allah has sent you Talut as king." They said, "How can he have kingship over us while we are more worthy of kingship than he, and he has not been given an abundance of wealth?" He said, "Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you and increased him broadly in knowledge and physical stature. And Allah gives His dominion to whom He wills, and Allah is all-Encompassing and Knowing"﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:247).

What is worthy of drawing attention to in this context is that Britain (Biritaniya) respects the system of monarchy until this present time, moved by this belief, and that there is no king except by Allah's granting him kingship, and that the kings of this world are by selection from Allah.

The verse points to what we are explaining: that the kings of this world do not own the affairs of their subjects, because Talut was made king, but he is not the owner of their property.

Whereas the dominion of Allah, exalted is He, is a dominion of creation, origination, and disposal, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He creates what He wills. He bestows female [children] upon whom He wills and bestows male [children] upon whom He wills, or He pairs them, males and females, and He renders whom He wills barren. Indeed, He is Knowing and Competent﴾ (Ash-Shura 42:49–50).

"Knowing and Competent" here is among His attributes, glorified is He, so He disposes of His dominion with knowledge and from complete power, glorified is He. ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He gives life and causes death, and He is over all things competent﴾ (Al-Hadid 57:2).

The reality of this becomes manifest when the true Day comes, when every dominion, small or great, vanishes, and every king, great or small, is humbled, and none remains but His dominion, exalted is He: ﴿The Day they will come forth, nothing of them concealed from Allah. "To whom belongs the dominion today?" "To Allah, the One, the Subduer"﴾ (Ghafir 40:16).

(p-177) And in Surat al-Fatihah: ﴿Owner of the Day of Recompense﴾ (Al-Fatihah 1:4).

The other recitation is: "King of the Day of Recompense" (Al-Fatihah 1:4).

In both recitations together there is an indication of the difference between the dominion of Allah and the dominion of the servants, like the difference between the absolute king and the relative king, since the relative king does not own, whereas the absolute King is the Pure King, in whose hand is the realm of all things, and to whom all creation returns.

Whoever has these attributes is the one deserving to be worshipped alone, glorified is He, and not to have anyone associated with Him. This is the emblem of the servant in the fifth pillar of Islam, when he enters the state of ihram (sacred consecration) by saying the talbiyah: "Indeed, the praise and the blessing are Yours, and the dominion; You have no partner."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿The God of mankind﴾.

This is the third level in the perfection of servitude and in affirming that Allah the Exalted alone is the One deserving worship (al-uluhiyyah).

This is the point of reference (al-ihalah) which Shaykh (may Allah have mercy on him and on us) intended, as appears to be the case. For when the servant acknowledges that Allah is his Lord and Creator, the One who bestows favours upon him, who brought him into existence from non-existence and nurtured him with blessings, and that he has no lord besides Him, then he progresses, through his knowledge and certainty, to acknowledging that his Lord is his Sovereign (malik) and the sole Disposer of his affairs, and that he himself possesses nothing alongside Allah, and that no one among those besides Allah possesses anything for him.

And that all the affairs of the entire universe are under His command, so no good reaches him except by His permission, and no harm is averted from him except by His command.

And it becomes certain that he is a owned servant belonging to the One in whose hand is the dominion (malakut) of the heavens and the earth. Through this knowledge he reaches the conclusion that whoever possesses these attributes is the only one deserving to be singled out for worship and divinity, there is no god except Him.

Thus at the end of the Noble Qur'an there is the drawing out (intizaf) of acknowledgment from the servant to Allah the Glorified, by way of obligation (ilzam), in the sense for which Allah sent His messengers and sent down His books, namely that Allah alone be worshipped. This is what the Shaykh explicitly stated in the earlier reference (ihalah).

And since the Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, drew attention to observing the end of the Noble Qur'an, if we return to the beginning and end of the Noble Qur'an we will find a wonderful linkage, for those three attributes in Surat an-Nas (p-178) are present in Surat al-Fatihah. Thus the conclusion agrees with the opening in this great meaning: in al-Fatihah ﴿All praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾ and ﴿Master of the Day of Judgment﴾. So the attributes of lordship (rububiyyah), dominion (mulk) and divinity (uluhiyyah) come in the word of majesty (lafz al-jalalah).

The noble conclusion is thus a case of "returning to the beginning" (awd ala al-bad'), and the whole Qur'an between them is an explanation and clarification of the measuring out of this great meaning.

Further clarification of this will come at the end, God willing, Exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 114, verse 4:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿From the evil of the whisperer (waswas), who withdraws (khannas)﴾.

Both are intensive forms (sighat mubalaghah) derived from al-waswasah (whispering) and al-khans (withdrawing), with the nun silent.

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon him and upon us, had already explained the meaning of al-waswasah and al-waswas linguistically and in the Sharia, namely at his discussion of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then Satan whispered to him, saying, "O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 120], and so on.

He explained their derivations and the root of their derivation, which revolves around the fact that al-waswasah is a hidden speech, and al-khans is delay (al-ta'akhkhur), as he discussed in his work Daf' Iham al-Idtirab (Removing the Appearance of Contradiction), where the two opposite meanings came together.

Because al-waswas is one who whispers much, in order to lead people astray through it, and al-khannas is one who much withdraws and turns back from leading people astray.

The answer is that every situation has its own statement: he whispers when the servant is heedless of the remembrance of his Lord, and he withdraws when the servant remembers his Lord, may He be exalted, as indicated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil, and he is his companion﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 36], to the end of it. End of quotation.

⁕ ⁕ ⁕

The author said in (Daf' Iham al-Idtirab 'an Ayat al-Kitab):

(p-468) In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Surah An-Nas

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿From the evil of the whisperer (waswas), who withdraws (khannas)﴾.

It is not hidden what contradiction lies between these two attributes with which this accursed, wicked one is described, for the waswas is one who whispers much in order to lead people astray, and the khannas is one who much withdraws and turns back from leading people astray.

The answer is that every situation has its own statement: he is a whisperer when the servant is heedless of the remembrance of his Lord, and a withdrawer when the servant remembers his Lord, may He be exalted, as indicated by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever turns away from the remembrance of the Most Merciful, We appoint for him a devil, and he is his companion﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 36], and so on.

And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe﴾ [An-Nahl: 99], and so on.

By the praise of Allah, may He be exalted, what we intended to compile has been completed in the city of the Prophet ﷺ. We ask Allah, may He be exalted, to grant us and our Muslim brothers success in statements and deeds, and to make our effort sincere for His Noble Face. Indeed He is Near, Responsive. Amin.

And may Allah send blessings and peace upon our Prophet Muhammad, his family and companions, and grant them peace.

(p-179) The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Who whispers into the breasts of mankind﴾.

It has been disputed here whether the adverbial phrase (ẓarf) refers to the whisperer at the time he whispers, so that he is present in the breasts and whispers to the heart, or whether it refers to the act of whispering itself. In that case, "breasts" means the hearts, since the hearts are located in the breasts, which is a figurative usage of naming the location while meaning what is in it (majāz, figurative speech), as is common in rhetorical styles.

This is like the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Then let him call upon his council﴾ [al-'Alaq: 17], where "council" (nādī) refers to the people who gather in it.

The Shaykh, may Allah's mercy be upon us and him, previously discussed the alternation of the verb "whisper" (waswasa) with "to" (ilā) at one time and with "to" (li, the lām) at another. In Sūrat al-A'rāf: ﴿Then Satan whispered to them both﴾ [al-A'rāf: 20], and in Ṭā Hā: ﴿Then Satan whispered to him﴾ [Ṭā Hā: 120].

The conclusion of what he mentioned in reconciling the two is one of two matters. Either the prepositions substitute for one another, and he cited examples for this, or the verb "whispered" means "for his sake," and "whispered to him" means "conveyed the whispering to him." But here Allah said ﴿in the breasts of mankind﴾ and did not say "to the breasts of mankind." So is this also a case of prepositions substituting for one another, or is it a pure adverbial phrase of place?

The apparent meaning is that it is an adverbial phrase. But is it an adverbial phrase for the whisperer, or an adverbial phrase for the whispering itself?

Looking at the statements of the commentators, the words of Ibn Jarir (al-Ṭabarī) allow for both meanings without specifying one.

As for al-Qurṭubī and al-Alūsī, they stated clearly what appeared to them and what they reached.

Al-Qurṭubī said: Muqātil said, "Satan is in the form of a pig that runs through the channels of the blood in the veins; Allah has empowered him over that." He also mentioned the hadith: "Indeed, Satan runs through the son of Adam as the blood runs, so narrow his channels."

He also said: Abū Tha'laba al-Khushanī said, "I asked my Lord to show me Satan and his place in the son of Adam. So I saw him: his hands were in his hands, his feet in his feet, and his [sensory] organs in his body, except that he had a snout like the snout of a dog. When he remembers Allah he withdraws, and when he falls silent from the remembrance of Allah, he seizes the heart."

As for al-Alūsī, he clearly stated the division we have presented. He said: ﴿Who whispers into the breasts of mankind﴾. It has been said: "Their hearts are meant figuratively."

Some said: Satan enters the chest, which is like the vestibule, and from it he casts what he wants to cast into the heart and conveys it to it. Nothing rationally prevents his entering the interior of a human being. He also cited the hadith: "Indeed, Satan runs..." to its end.

(p-180) By "figurative" (majāz) he means what we presented earlier: naming the location while meaning what resides in it.

Ibn Kathīr mentioned from Ibn 'Abbās and Mujāhid that Satan squats upon the heart of the son of Adam; when he becomes heedless and forgetful, he whispers, and when he remembers Allah, he withdraws.

What appears to me, and Allah knows best, is that the breast is the adverbial phrase for the whispering, and that it (Satan) casts the whispering into the heart, according to what Ibn 'Abbās and Mujāhid, may Allah have mercy on them both, said.

As for the word "mankind" here, the noun to which "breasts" is attached: there is a difference regarding what is meant by it. It has been said: it refers to humankind, which is the more commonly used sense.

It has also been said: it refers to both jinn and humans (al-thaqalān, the two weighty species).

Indeed, using "mankind" for the species (jins) is attested, as al-Qurṭubī related. He said, concerning some Arabs, that a man was narrating and a group of jinn came and stood still, so it was said to them: "Who are you?" They said: "People (nās) from among the jinn." This is the meaning of the words of al-Farrā'.

The proponent of this view argued by analogy from the use of the two words rijāl (men) and nafar (group) in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And there were men from mankind who sought refuge with men from the jinn﴾ [al-Jinn: 6], and His words: ﴿And when We turned towards you a group of the jinn﴾.

On this basis, the whisper from which refuge is sought would whisper into the breasts of both jinn and humans.

Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyya mentioned this view, but he rejected it and declared it weak, because the word "mankind" is more apparent and more well-known for humans, and that is what is familiar in the Qur'anic usage. Moreover, on this view the Qur'an would be dividing a thing into a part of itself, because it would make "mankind" a counterpart to the jinn, while making the jinn a type of mankind. End of quotation, summarized.

In any case, the methodology of Adwā' al-Bayān is that when something is open to more than one meaning, and the majority of the Qur'an's usages of a word correspond to one of the two possibilities, the frequency of its usage is a preponderant factor. All of the Qur'an's usages of the word "mankind" refer exclusively to humans, and it was never used even once for the jinn, despite its occurring five times in this sūrah alone, which is why it is named Sūrat al-Nās.

(p-181) As for the analogy with the two words rajul (man) and nafar (group), Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyya also rejected it, on the grounds that they occurred qualified: "men from the jinn" and "a group from the jinn." But when unqualified, they did not occur. Likewise, the word "mankind" may be used qualified, as "people from the jinn," but not unqualified.

On this basis, wherever the word "mankind" occurs here without qualification, it cannot be interpreted as referring to both jinn and humans together. Rather, it is specific to humans alone, and "in the breasts of mankind" means in the breasts of humans.

Abū al-Su'ūd mentioned another meaning for the word "mankind": that it is "those who forget" (al-nāsī), from forgetfulness (al-nisyān), with the yā' deleted for lightness, because the whisperer only whispers at times of forgetfulness and heedlessness.

On this view, the deletion of the yā' is like its deletion in "the caller" (al-dā'ī) in the words: ﴿On the day the caller calls﴾ [al-Qamar: 6] and similar instances.

However, on this view it remains to be explained who is meant by "the forgetful one": is he from humans or from jinn? So it does not escape the two previous possibilities. Moreover, this view is a necessary consequence of the meaning of "the whisperer, the withdrawer" (al-waswās al-khannās).

This view is also met with an objection: the plural "breasts" and the singular "mankind." A plural is only attached to a plural, meaning the plural of "breasts," because a singular has no plural of "breasts." So the plural must be matched with a plural, or one singular with a singular.

Something has come in the attachment of a plural to a dual in the words: ﴿For your hearts have swerved﴾ [al-Taḥrīm: 4].

Abū Ḥayyān said: Its beauty lies in the fact that the dual is a plural in meaning, and the plural in such a case is more used than the dual, and the dual is less than the plural.

As the poet said:

"So they both exchanged their souls with glances like the windows of the sacrificed camels which are not raised."

(p-182) This would have been the analogy, namely that the one who speaks of a dual uses a dual, but they disliked the combination of two duals, so they turned to the plural, since the dual is a plural in meaning and in form. This is not permissible according to our companions except in poetry.

Such as his words:

"O dove of the valley between the two valleys, sing."

He means "the valley of the two valleys." Ibn Mālik erred in al-Tas-hīl when he said: "We prefer the singular over the dual form." So you see that he erred Ibn Mālik in his preference for permitting the attachment of a plural to a singular, just as he said: "That is not permissible except in poetry," and that the attachment to a dual is for disliking the combination of two duals. Thus the invalidity of the words of Abū al-Su'ūd becomes clear.

As for the preferred of the two possibilities for the meaning of "mankind" mentioned earlier, it is the first possibility, namely that they are humans. And the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿From the jinn and mankind﴾ [al-Nās: 6] explain who carries out the whispering, that is, they explain the whisperer, the withdrawer, and that it comes from each of the two: the whispering of the jinn and the whispering of mankind.

This is evident from several matters. Among them: the address is to the Messenger (ﷺ) and to his community following him, so it is more apparent regarding humans.

Among them: if we were to make the first "mankind" general for whoever is whispered to, then "from the jinn and mankind" would make the source of the whispering both jinn and humans, so it would follow that among the whispering of humans is one who whispers into the breasts of jinn. This is far-fetched.

Among them: if the word "mankind" included both jinn and humans, there would be no need for this division, "the jinn and mankind," and it would have been sufficient in the second to suffice with what was sufficient in the first. The one who whispers into the breasts of mankind would be from mankind. But instead, the location of the whispering is explained, "the breasts of mankind," and then the source of the whispering is mentioned, "the jinn and mankind." And Allah knows best.

* *

A note.

Ibn Ḥayyān (Abū Ḥayyān) mentioned at the end of his tafsīr a subtle comparison between the two sūrahs of refuge (al-Mu'awwidhatayn), saying: "Since the harm to religion, which is the calamity of whispering, is greater than the harm to this world, however great it may be, the construction in seeking refuge from it came with three attributes: the Lord, the King, and the God, even though the sought-after object is one."

(p-183) "In seeking refuge from three things: the Darkness when it settles, the blowers in knots, and the envier when he envies, with one attribute, which is the Lord, even though the thing sought refuge from is multiple."

"This other is a noble observation, which I have long looked forward to from two standpoints: one between the two sūrahs, and the other between Sūrat al-Nās and the order of the noble Mushaf. Their presentation will come, Allah willing."

"However, from the standpoint of Abū Ḥayyān, namely that in Sūrat al-Falaq He, the Exalted, sought refuge with one attribute, which is ﴿the Lord of the daybreak﴾."

"In Sūrat al-Nās, He sought refuge with three attributes, even though what is sought refuge from in the first is three matters, and what is sought refuge from in the second is one matter. Because of the gravity of the single matter, the three attributes came."

"It is also said from another angle: what is sought refuge from in the first sūrah are matters that come from outside a person and reach him as aggression from others. These may be manifest evils, and such can often be guarded against or avoided before they occur, and shunned once known. Whereas the single evil in the second comes to him from within, and may be the stirrings of the self and what he cannot repel, since Satan sees us and we do not see him, as in the words: ﴿Indeed, he sees you, he and his tribe, from where you do not see them﴾ [al-A'rāf: 27]."

"He may stir up against him the passing thoughts of his soul and the impulses of his mind, so he finds no escape from them except by seeking refuge and taking shelter in the Lord of mankind, King of mankind, God of mankind."

"As for the two standpoints I mentioned: the first is between the two sūrahs, and it is among what Abū Ḥayyān presented. In Sūrat al-Falaq He said: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾ [al-Falaq: 1], and the Lord of the daybreak is equivalent to His words ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, because there is nothing in this existence but that it is split off from something else."

"In the crops: ﴿Splitter of the grain and the date-stone﴾ [al-An'ām: 95]."

"In time: ﴿Splitter of the dawn﴾ [al-An'ām: 96]."

(p-184) "In living beings: ﴿He who created you from a single soul and created from it its mate and spread from them both many men and women﴾ [al-Nisā': 1]."

"In inanimate things, His words, the Exalted, point to it: ﴿Have not those who disbelieved seen that the heavens and the earth were a joined mass, then We parted them, and made from water every living thing? Will they not believe?﴾ ﴿And We placed in the earth firm mountains lest it shake with them﴾ [al-Anbiyā': 30–31]."

"So the Lord of the daybreak is equivalent to the Lord of the worlds. Thus in seeking refuge He matched it with the generality of what is sought refuge from: ﴿From the evil of what He created﴾."

"Then the mention of the specific came after the general, for emphasis on it: ﴿from the evil of the darkness when it settles﴾, ﴿the blowers in knots﴾, and ﴿the envier when he envies﴾."

"So what is sought refuge in is one attribute, and what is sought refuge from is the generality of what He created, in totality and in detail. Whereas in the second sūrah, what is sought refuge in are three attributes, which are the attributes of majesty of Allah, the Exalted: the Lord, the King, and the God."

"He matched what is sought refuge from, which is one thing only, namely the whispering, the withdrawer. This indicates the severity of the danger of what is sought refuge from."

"And that is so, because if we look at the reality of the matter, we will find that the source of every trial and the origin of every evil, sooner or later, is due to the whispering, the withdrawer. And it is connected to the history of the existence of humankind."

"The first offense committed against the first human was indeed from this whispering, the withdrawer. For when Allah, the Exalted, honored Ādam, creating him with His own hand, made the angels prostrate to him, and settled him in the Garden, he and his wife, where he would neither hunger nor go naked, neither thirst nor be exposed to the sun, and they would eat from it freely wherever they wished, except from the forbidden tree, then Satan whispered to them both until they ate from it, and he led them on by deception, until they were both sent down from it, some of them enemies to others."

Commentary of al-Shinqiti (Adwa' al-Bayan) on surah 114, verse 5 (part 2 of 3):

After they settled on the earth, [Iblis] went to their two sons, Qabil and Habil, and tempted them too, until the soul of one of them made him willing to kill his brother, and he became one of the regretful. (p-185)

Thus he does with all of mankind throughout their lives, tempting them, so that he confuses them in this world and destroys them in the Hereafter. He has taken woman as a bridge to everything he wants. And here he returns to the attempt to strip our parents of their clothing in Paradise: he strips them of it in the shade of the Sacred House of God during their circumambulation before the Prophethood, and he continues to seduce [mankind] through the way of woman, in every time and place, to take them out of uprightness, just as he took their parents out of Paradise.

He continues to bring against man his cavalry and his infantry, boldly keeping his oath before God by His might: "I will surely mislead them all" [Sad: 82].

The most dangerous gateways to corruption in societies are those concerning wealth, blood, or honour, as in the hadith of the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Verily your blood, your wealth, and your honour are sacred to you, as the sanctity of this day of yours" and so on to its end.

Has any crime against any one of these ever occurred except through the influence of the Whispering, the Withdrawing [Waswas al-Khannas]? No, by God, never.

And so it is in the Hereafter.

God has clarified the position explicitly in the eloquent and plain statement of Satan: "And Satan will say when the matter has been decided: Indeed, God promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you, but I failed you. I had over you no authority except that I invited you, and you responded to me. So do not blame me; blame yourselves. I cannot help you, nor can you help me. Indeed, I disbelieve in your association of me [with God] before" [Ibrahim: 22], to the end of the verse.

The enemy of the Muslims has known that the most dangerous weapon against man is doubt, and there is no path to it except through whispering. So he took over Iblis's mission and began whispering to the Muslims about their religion and their worldly affairs, casting doubt on their ability to live a dignified life independent of him, casting doubt on their ability to advance and to achieve true independence, and even on their capacity for innovation and invention, so that they remain in his orbit and within the circle of his influence. The Muslims thus continue to revolve in a vicious circle, advancing one foot and delaying the other.

Whoever doubts the outcome of a deed will never undertake it; rather, what he builds today he demolishes tomorrow. This dangerous result was announced by the president of the Congress of Orientalists in the Middle East more than thirty years ago, when the congress convened in (Beirut) to present the results of their work and study their methods of missionary activity.

(p-186) The participants complained that, after about forty years of their continuous work, they had not been able to convert a single Muslim to Christianity. The president of the congress said: "If we have not been able to convert a Muslim, we have nevertheless been able to create a wavering in opinion, and so we have succeeded in our work."

This is the method of the enemy: casting doubt on the matters of Islam in order to create wavering in the faith of the Muslims, sometimes through inheritance, sometimes through polygamy, through the motives for fighting, through the enslavement of slaves, and so on.

Until some of the sons of the Muslims came to exceed the limits of doubt into assent, and began to call to what the enemy calls to. All of this is nothing but the harvest and the results of the Withdrawing Whisperer.

It is therefore no wonder that the three glorious attributes are combined: "the Lord of mankind" [30] "the King of mankind" [30] "the God of mankind."

This is the first viewpoint regarding the surahs al-Falaq and an-Nas.

As for the second viewpoint, which concerns the relation between surah an-Nas and the arrangement of the noble Mushaf, with His saying, may He be exalted: "Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds. The Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful. Sovereign of the Day of Recompense. You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help. Guide us to the straight path. The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour" [al-Fatihah: 2–7].

In this noble beginning there is the instilling of tranquillity in the heart, expressed by praise, the sign of contentment, happiness, and acknowledgment of God's lordship; then faith in the Resurrection and the acknowledgment that God is the Owner of the Day of Recompense; then commitment to worship God alone and turning to Him, seeking His help, asking Him to guide to the straight path, and asking for the company of those upon whom He has bestowed favour.

Immediately after this, at the beginning of surah al-Baqarah, comes: "That is the Book; there is no doubt in it; it is guidance for the God-fearing" [al-Baqarah: 2]. That is: the guidance you seek to the straight path is in this Book, there is no doubt in it. Then He explained who the God-fearing are, upon whom God has bestowed favour, with His saying: "Who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and spend from what We have provided them. And who believe in what has been revealed to you and what was revealed before you, and of the Hereafter they are certain" [al-Baqarah: 3–4].

And once again, for emphasis: those alone are "upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful" [al-Baqarah: 5].

(p-187) Then the surah proceeds calmly to divide people into three categories: believers, disbelievers, and the wavering between them, who are the hypocrites.

Then comes the explicit call, which is the first call in the Mushaf addressed to all mankind: "O mankind, worship your Lord" [al-Baqarah: 21], and it establishes proofs of His right to worship and of the possibility of resurrection with His saying: "Who created you and those before you, that you may become God-fearing. Who made for you the earth a bed and the sky a canopy, and sent down from the sky water, and brought forth thereby fruits as provision for you. So do not attribute to God equals while you know" [al-Baqarah: 21–22].

After establishing the principle, which is belief, the surah goes on to mention the branches of Islam. It includes all the pillars of Islam and many matters of transactions and jihad, and there is hardly a chapter of jurisprudence that has no mention in this surah. What follows it explains what was summarised in it or what is mentioned within it.

And so on, until the Qur'an ends with the completion of the Sharia and the perfection of the religion.

As for the description of the God-fearing who are guided, at the beginning of the Mushaf, that they believe in the unseen, and among it is belief in the Last Day and what it contains of reckoning, punishment and reward, the matters of the unseen require certainty, so that the reward or punishment may be established upon them.

Reward and punishment are the result of doing and of abstaining.

Doing and abstaining are the basis of obligation, because a person complies with a command in hope of reward, and refrains from what is forbidden out of fear of punishment.

So it seems that the arrangement of the noble Mushaf points to what must be noticed: the Qur'an began with praise, as thanksgiving to God for the blessing He bestowed upon man by sending it down and sending the Messenger who carries it. Then it moved him from the world to the Hereafter, which is greater in worth and weight. Then it drew for him the path taken by the guided, the people of favour and contentment. Then it halted him upon it so that he would follow their way.

And so on, until He brought him, after the completion of clarification, guidance and direction, to the end of this straight path, and halted him there to say to him: when you are at peace with this religion, believe in God, Lord of the worlds, (p-188) believe in the coming of the Day of Recompense, know the path of the guided, see the three categories of people, believers, disbelievers and hypocrites, and the end of each of them, then hold fast to this Book, walk this path, accompany the people of favour, avoid those upon whom is anger and those who are astray, beware of the way of the hypocrites who doubt, and take utmost care against what causes all of that, which is the Withdrawing Whisperer, who would cast doubt on you regarding the objects of faith, or on the straightness of your path and its uprightness, or on the infallibility and perfection of your Book. Be certain of what you are upon. Do not forget his danger to your two parents before you, for they were in Paradise, the abode of peace, and were not safe from him; he lured them with deception. So beware of him, seek refuge in Me whenever he assails you or a visitation from him touches you, and be like your righteous predecessors: "When a visitation from Satan touches them, they remember, and then they see clearly" [al-A'raf: 201].

You have known his enmity towards you from before, and his enmity arises from envy.

It seems that the connection between the two surahs points to the source of that enmity and its link to this warning. In the first: "And from the evil of an envier when he envies," so Satan envied Adam for the honour God had given him, as we have previously mentioned.

An enemy who envies is not satisfied except by the removal of the blessing from the one envied. And although Adam's repentance was the way to his salvation, as in His saying: "Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He accepted his repentance" [al-Baqarah: 37].

So your salvation too is in words by which you seek refuge from your enemy: "In the Lord of mankind, the King of mankind, the God of mankind." For the Lord is the One who shows mercy to His servants; the King of mankind is the One who protects them, guards them and watches over them; and the God of mankind is the One to whom they devote worship, humble themselves, and seek refuge, glorified is He.

* *

Note

If all of this is the danger of the Withdrawing Whisperer from among the jinn and mankind, and they are a common enemy, waiting in ambush, spiteful and envious, then what is the way to be saved from him?

What appears, and God knows best, is that the way to salvation rests on two matters:

The first: it is derived from the general principles of the Book and the Sunnah.

(p-189) The second: I heard it from my shaykh, may God's mercy be upon him and upon us.

As for the first: since the task of whispering is to create doubt, wavering and hesitation, the general principles of obligation require the Muslim to act with resolve, certainty and pursuit without hesitation, as in His saying: "And when you have decided, then rely upon God" [Al 'Imran: 159], and He praised some of the messengers for their resolve and commanded following them: "So be patient as the messengers of resolve were patient" [al-Ahqaf: 35].

The Prophet ﷺ said: "Leave what makes you doubt for what does not make you doubt."

The jurisprudential maxim is: "Certainty is not removed by doubt."

And the hadith: "Satan comes to one of you while he is in prayer and blows wind into his rear, so that he imagines he has broken wind when he has not. So he should not leave [the prayer] until he hears a sound or smells something."

For this reason all obligations are based on certainty. Beliefs necessarily require certainty.

Acts of worship in their branches necessarily require intention: "Actions are only by intentions."

The condition of intention is resolve and certainty. So if one intends prayer on the condition that if so-and-so arrives he will abandon it, his intention is not valid. If one intends fasting on the condition that if he wishes he will break it, his fast is not valid.

Malik stated in the Muwatta' (a collection of hadith by Malik ibn Anas) that if on the day of doubt (the last day of Sha'ban) one intends in the night to fast the next day on the condition that if it turns out to be from Ramadan it is for Ramadan, and otherwise it is a voluntary fast, his fast is not valid either as obligatory or voluntary, and even if Ramadan comes, it does not count for him from it, and he must make it up, because there was no resolve in the intention.

As for Hajj: if one intends it, it becomes binding on him and he must proceed with it, and he does not have the power to leave it by his own choice.

Likewise, transactions in all contracts are based on resolve, even in jest and play; some are binding, such as marriage, divorce and manumission.

From all of this it follows that the motives for determination are drawn from the obligations, which overcome the impulses of doubt and hesitation, and no room remained in the heart of the believer for doubt, nor place for whispering.

Satan used to flee from the path of 'Umar, may God be pleased with him.

(p-190) As for what I heard from my shaykh, may God's mercy be upon him and upon us, it is his saying: God has taught us how to guard against the enemy from among mankind and from among the jinn.

As for the enemy from mankind, it is in His saying: "The good and the evil are not equal. Repel [evil] with that which is better, and thereupon the one between whom and you there is enmity will become as though he were a devoted friend" [Fussilat: 34].

This shows that confronting an enemy's harm with goodness towards him removes his enmity and wins his friendship, as He said: "Repel with that which is better the evil."

As for the enemy from the jinn, it is in His saying: "And if there comes to you from Satan an incitement, then seek refuge in God. Indeed, He is the Hearing, the Knowing" [Fussilat: 36].

This is what is indicated by the narrations mentioned earlier, that the Shaytan withdraws when he hears the remembrance of Allah.

As for His saying, may Allah have mercy on him: "The Shaytan of the jinn is repelled by seeking refuge in Allah from him, and that suffices him, because the plot of Shaytan was weak."

As for the Shaytan of mankind, he is in need of diplomacy (muṣānaʿah), repelling (mudāfaʿah), and patience towards him, as indicated by the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And none is granted it except those who are patient, and none is granted it except one of great fortune.﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 35].

May Allah, the Exalted, grant us and all the Muslims a great fortune in this world and the Hereafter; indeed He is the One asked, and the best one hoped in.

Ibn Kathir narrated the hadith of Abu Sa'id, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) "used to seek refuge from the evil eyes of the jinn and mankind. When the two Mu'awwidhatayn were revealed, he took hold of them and left whatever else." Narrated by at-Tirmidhi, an-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah, and at-Tirmidhi said: "Hasan sahih."

And it is narrated "from Abdullah al-Aslami, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) placed his hand on his chest and then said: 'Say.' I did not know what to say. Then he said to me: 'Say.' I said: 'He is Allah, the One.' Then he said to me: Say. I said: 'I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak from the evil of what He has created,' until I finished it. Then he said to me: Say. I said: 'I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind,' until I finished it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Thus, seek refuge; for those who seek refuge have never sought refuge with the like of these two ever.'"

(p-191) All praise is due to Allah, first and last, and may Allah send blessings upon the best of His creation and the most honoured of them before Him, the one whom He chose for His message, honoured us with his sending, sealed His messengers with him, ennobled us through him, and guided us to follow him; and upon his family and companions, the good and pure, and those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgement, and upon us along with them all. Indeed, He is All-Hearing, Responsive.
